capitals.note: 'Capital and largest city: Warsaw'. The government left Warsaw 'in the first days of the campaign' of 1939 and reached Lublin on 6 September (Invasion of Poland page); the government-in-exile was set up in Paris and later London.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's row starts in 1919 but the state's 'Establishment' is 11 November 1918 (it 'existed between 7 October 1918 and 6 October 1939'). The 1919 shape is borrowed for the last weeks of 1918, when the Polish-Ukrainian fighting in Lwow (from 1 November) and the Greater Poland uprising were under way; unverified: page budget.

keyframe_review.note: 223,596 km2 is 0.58 of the infobox's 388,634 km2 and omits what Poland held by the end of 1919: the shape holds 1 of the 198 cells of Eastern Galicia and 38 of 174 Volhynian cells, but 'Poland won the disputed territory on 18 July 1919' and 'The Polish offensive resulted in a takeover of the western part of the province' [Volhynia] (Polish-Soviet War page). Add both for the year-end state; Vilnius, Pinsk and Grodno, which Polish forces also held, are not on the pages for 1919.

373,273 km2, ratio 0.96 to the infobox's 388,634 km2 (the body gives 389,720 km2 after the Trans-Olza annexation; no year for either). This is the Riga frontier: 'Poland retained control of modern-day Western Ukraine and Western Belarus' (Treaty of Riga, 18 March 1921; ceasefire 18 October 1920), 'about 200 km east of the Curzon Line'. The summer-1920 retreat to Warsaw and the Kyiv episode are in the ledger. Eastern Galicia was recognised only by the ambassadors of 14 March 1923. The Vilnius area and Cieszyn Silesia are partly inside the shape (see ledger).
373,209 km2: unchanged within the shape's precision (-64 km2); no territorial event on the pages between the Vilnius annexation of 24 March 1922 and 1938.

373,079 km2 (-130 km2): the state before Trans-Olza. On 1 October 1938 Poland 'annexed an area of 801.5 km2 with a population of 227,399 people'; the 1939 shape (+1,001 km2) holds it, so the year-end 1938 state is the 1939 shape. The ledger carries the October event.

374,080 km2, ratio 0.96 to the body's 389,720 km2 'after the Trans-Olza annexation'. The shape is the state on 1 September 1939; the German and Soviet partition (8 October annexation, General Government, 17 September Soviet invasion) is in the ledger.

region.text: Greater Poland, Posen

ledger.note: Late 1918: the Greater Poland uprising. 'another war of national liberation began under the banner of the Greater Poland uprising (1918-1919)'; the page gives the years only.

region.text: the Polish lands freed by the end of the war: the former Congress Poland and Western Galicia, with Greater Poland rising

ledger.note: 11 November 1918: Poland is reborn. The infobox gives 'End of the First World War: 11 November 1918' as the establishment and 'existed between 7 October 1918 and 6 October 1939'; the page does not say independence was declared on that date.

region.text: Eastern Galicia, including Lwow and the Drohobych oil fields

ledger.note: 1 November 1918: the Polish-Ukrainian War begins in Lwow. 'The Polish-Ukrainian War broke out in Lwow (1 November 1918)'; Ukrainian units 'took control over Lviv' that night.

region.text: the western part of Volhynia, Kowel and Wlodzimierz Wolynski

ledger.note: 1919: Poland takes western Volhynia. 'The Polish offensive resulted in a takeover of the western part of the province' [Volhynia]; the Polish-Ukrainian War page adds that Kowel and Wlodzimierz Wolynski passed from Austrian commanders to Polish committees in the winter of 1918-1919. No month on either page.

region.text: the disputed part of Cieszyn Silesia

ledger.note: 23 January 1919: Czechoslovakia invades Cieszyn Silesia. On 5 November 1918 the area 'was divided between Poland and Czechoslovakia by an agreement of the two councils'; 'the Czechs decided to resolve the issue by force and on 23 January 1919 invaded the area'; ceasefire on 3 February.

minus.text: Eastern Galicia, including Lwow and the Drohobych oil fields

region.text: Western Belarus and Western Ukraine, the 1920 shape east of the Bug without Eastern Galicia

ledger.note: 14 February 1919: the Polish-Soviet War begins. 'The Polish-Soviet War (14 February 1919 - 18 March 1921) was fought primarily between' Poland and Soviet Russia; 'the first Polish-Soviet military clashes' came in the east (Vilnius Region page).

region.text: Pomerelia (the Polish Corridor) and Greater Poland (Posen)

ledger.note: June 1919: the Treaty of Versailles gives Poland the Corridor and Posen. 'The victorious Allies of the First World War confirmed the rebirth of Poland in the Treaty of Versailles of June 1919'; 'a short strip of coastline known as the Polish Corridor'. The page gives no transfer date; the German dossier dates the loss to the treaty's entry into force on 10 January 1920.

region.text: Greater Poland, Posen

ledger.note: 1919: the Greater Poland uprising ends in Polish hands; the page gives only the span (1918-1919) and the Treaty of Versailles of June 1919.

region.text: Eastern Galicia, including Lwow and the Drohobych oil fields

ledger.note: 18 July 1919: Poland wins Eastern Galicia. 'Poland won the disputed territory on 18 July 1919'; the Ukrainian army fell back to the Zbruch line on 16-18 July.

region.text: Eastern Galicia, including Lwow and the Drohobych oil fields

ledger.note: 18 July 1919: Poland takes Eastern Galicia. 'Poland won the disputed territory on 18 July 1919', 'after which ZUNR was occupied by Poland'; the Allied council 'legitimized Polish control' of the land up to the Zbruch on 25 June 1919; the Council of Ambassadors incorporated it into Poland on 14 March 1923 (the page's date).

region.text: Upper Silesia

ledger.note: August 1919: the first Silesian Uprising. 'in August 1919, Polish-speaking residents of Upper Silesia initiated a series of three Silesian Uprisings'.

region.text: the Vilnius area, taken by 'a staged mutiny by Lucjan Zeligowski'

ledger.note: Autumn 1920: Zeligowski's mutiny creates Central Lithuania under Polish protection. The Poles took control after 'a staged mutiny by Lucjan Zeligowski' (the page gives 'autumn 1920', not the 9 October date); Lithuania 'refused to recognize this action or the border'.

region.text: the Vilnius area

ledger.note: Autumn 1920: the Vilnius dispute with Lithuania. 'following Polish military action in autumn 1920' the line became a de facto frontier; Lithuania never recognised it before the Polish ultimatum of 1938.

region.text: Kiev

ledger.note: 7 May 1920: Poland and its Ukrainian allies take Kyiv. 'On 7 May, Polish and allied Ukrainian forces captured Kiev' in the offensive launched in April after the alliance of 21 April 1920 with Symon Petliura (Polish-Ukrainian War page).

region.text: Kiev

ledger.note: June 1920: the Soviet counter-offensive. 'the Soviet Red Army launched a successful counteroffensive starting in June 1920'; 'By August, Soviet troops had pushed Polish forces back to Warsaw'; the page does not date the loss of Kyiv.

region.text: the disputed part of Cieszyn Silesia

ledger.note: 28 July 1920: the Spa Conference divides Cieszyn Silesia. 'the Spa Conference (also known as the Conference of Ambassadors) divided each of the three disputed areas between Poland and Czechoslovakia'.

region.text: the disputed part of Cieszyn Silesia

ledger.note: 28 July 1920: Czechoslovakia receives the larger part of Cieszyn Silesia. It received '58.1% of the area of Cieszyn Silesia, containing 67.9% of the population'; Poland kept the rest (41.9% by arithmetic). The loss is measured against the agreement of 5 November 1918, which the Czechoslovak invasion overturned; the Czechoslovak dossier records the same step as its gain.

ledger.note: 18 March 1921: the Peace of Riga ends the war. 'the official treaty ending the war was signed on 18 March 1921' after the ceasefire of 18 October 1920; the war ended 'in a decisive Polish victory'.

region.text: Western Belarus and Western Ukraine, the 1920 shape east of the Bug without Eastern Galicia

ledger.note: 18 March 1921: Riga leaves Poland Western Belarus and Western Ukraine. 'Poland retained control of modern-day Western Ukraine and Western Belarus'; 'Poland's eastern border was established about 200 km east of the Curzon Line' (the provisional boundary of 8 December 1919).

region.text: the Vilnius Region (Central Lithuania), about 32,250 km2 on the Vilnius Region page

ledger.note: 24 March 1922: Poland annexes Central Lithuania. 'it was annexed by Poland on 24 March 1922 thus finalizing Poland's claims over the territory'; the Second Polish Republic page: 'after the annexation of the Republic of Central Lithuania'.

region.text: the Vilnius area

ledger.note: 24 March 1922: Central Lithuania ceases to be a separate state, annexed by Poland.

region.text: the Vilnius area

ledger.note: 24 March 1922: the de facto end of the fight for Vilnius; Lithuania did not recognise the annexation until after the Polish ultimatum of 1938.

region.text: eastern Upper Silesia

ledger.note: 1922: Upper Silesia is partitioned. Bridging a silence: the page gives the three Silesian Uprisings from August 1919 but no plebiscite or partition; the date and the Polish share are the German dossier's (loss to the Second Polish Republic in May 1922).

region.text: Upper Silesia

ledger.note: 1922: the fighting over Upper Silesia ends in the partition (bridged from the German dossier; this page does not date the end).

region.text: Trans-Olza (Zaolzie), the part of Cieszyn Silesia east of the Olza held by Czechoslovakia; 801.5 km2

ledger.note: 1 October 1938: Poland annexes Trans-Olza. 'At noon on 30 September, Poland gave an ultimatum to the Czechoslovak government' and the Polish Army 'annexed an area of 801.5 km2 with a population of 227,399 people' (the Czechoslovak dossier dates it 2 October). Germany annexed it on 26 October 1939.

region.text: Gorna Orawa and Tatranska Javorina

ledger.note: 1939: Slovakia seizes areas on Poland's southern border. 'Slovakia seized areas along Poland's southern border - including Gorna Orawa and Tatranska Javorina' (the Invasion of Poland page says Slovakia 'gained back those territories taken by Poland in autumn 1938'); the Slovak dossier dates it 21 November 1939. [Reviewer eu-21-b, 2026-11-01: month set to 9: the page ties the seizure to the start of the invasion ('On that day, Germany and Slovakia attacked Poland', 1 September 1939); the Slovak dossier's November date is the formal annexation.]

region.text: the whole of Poland

ledger.note: 1 September 1939: Germany invades Poland. 'The invasion began on 1 September 1939 when Germany marched into Poland'; the government 'left Warsaw in the first days of the campaign'.

region.text: eastern Poland up to the line of the rivers Narew, Bug, Vistula and San; the page puts the Soviet areas into the Byelorussian and Ukrainian republics

ledger.note: 17 September 1939: the Soviet Union invades. 'On 17 September the Soviet Union invaded as well, acting on a secret protocol of the pact'.

region.text: eastern Poland up to the line of the rivers Narew, Bug, Vistula and San; the page puts the Soviet areas into the Byelorussian and Ukrainian republics

ledger.note: 28 September 1939: the German-Soviet line is fixed. 'On 28 September, another secret German-Soviet protocol modified the arrangements of August'; the Red Army reached 'the line of rivers Narew, Bug, Vistula and San by 28 September'. Warsaw held out until that day.

region.text: eastern Poland up to the line of the rivers Narew, Bug, Vistula and San; the page puts the Soviet areas into the Byelorussian and Ukrainian republics

ledger.note: September 1939: eastern Poland falls to the Soviet Union. Its areas were incorporated 'into its constituent Byelorussian and Ukrainian republics'; the page gives no date for the incorporation (the Soviet dossier says 17-28 September for the occupation).

region.text: the whole of Poland

ledger.note: 6 October 1939: organised resistance ends. Polish forces surrendered 'after the four-day Battle of Kock near Lublin on 6 October, marking the end of the September Campaign'.

region.text: the western parts of Poland annexed on 8 October 1939 (the page names no provinces; the Wartheland, Danzig-West Prussia and Upper Silesia are the researcher's reading)

ledger.note: 8 October 1939: Germany annexes western Poland. 'On 8 October, Germany formally annexed the western parts of Poland.' The page names neither the decree nor the provinces.

region.text: the remaining block placed 'under the administration of the newly established General Government'

ledger.note: October 1939: the General Government is set up over the rest. The remaining block was placed 'under the administration of the newly established General Government' (this page dates its creation to 8 October; the General Government dossier gives 26 October 1939). The General Government has its own dossier and is run as occupied land by Germany.

region.text: the whole of Poland

ledger.note: 6 October 1939: the Second Polish Republic ends. 'Open organised Polish resistance ended on 6 October 1939'; the state 'existed between 7 October 1918 and 6 October 1939'; the government-in-exile was set up in Paris and later London after the fall of France in 1940.

wars.note: The page names the uprising '(1918-1919)' and gives no dates.

wars.name: Silesian Uprisings
wars.outcome: Three uprisings from August 1919; the partition of 1922 gave Poland the east of Upper Silesia (partition date from the German dossier).
wars.note: This page gives the August 1919 start only.

zones.text: the disputed part of Cieszyn Silesia

wars.outcome: Czechoslovak invasion of 23 January 1919, ceasefire of 3 February, Spa division of 28 July 1920 (Czechoslovakia 58.1%).
wars.note: Trans-Olza passed to Poland on 1 October 1938 and to Germany on 26 October 1939.

wars.name: Polish-Soviet War

minus.text: Eastern Galicia, including Lwow and the Drohobych oil fields

zones.text: Western Belarus and Western Ukraine, the 1920 shape east of the Bug without Eastern Galicia

wars.outcome: Polish victory at Warsaw (12-25 August 1920); the Peace of Riga of 18 March 1921 left Poland Western Ukraine and Western Belarus, about 200 km east of the Curzon Line.
wars.note: Kyiv fell to Poland on 7 May 1920; the Red Army counter-offensive began in June.

wars.name: Invasion of Poland
wars.outcome: Germany invaded on 1 September, the Soviet Union on 17 September; the partition line was fixed on 28 September and organised resistance ended on 6 October 1939.
wars.note: Germany annexed the west on 8 October; the General Government covered the rest of the German share.

certainty.note: The frontiers were being fixed by fighting (Greater Poland, Eastern Galicia, Cieszyn, Upper Silesia, the Soviet front).

Versailles (June 1919), Spa (28 July 1920), Riga (18 March 1921) and the ambassadors' decision of 14 March 1923 fixed the lines; the Lithuanian line (Vilnius) was never recognised by Lithuania until 1938, the Trans-Olza line is a 1938 ultimatum line.
The front and the partition line of 28 September are approximate.

notes: Cliopatria row 'Second Polish Republic' (1919-1939) is one state; the Wikidata id is unshared. 'Polish Armed Forces' (1918, a separate row in another batch) is not merged. Not on the pages opened (recorded at confidence 1 or left out): the transfer date of Posen and Pomerelia (10 January 1920), the Upper Silesia partition (1922) and its plebiscite, the Spisz and Orava arbitration of 1920 (a Trianon-page item, Czechoslovak land), the treaty of 1923 recognising the eastern frontier on 15 March 1923 (the Ukrainian war page gives 14 March 1923), Belarus 1919 (Grodno, Pinsk, Vilnius held by Polish forces) and the date of Vilnius's loss to Soviet forces in September 1939. Counterparts needing a dossier: central-lithuania (October 1920 - March 1922, a Polish-backed state at Vilnius). Region names the gazetteer lacks: 'Cieszyn' (a place; Cieszyn Silesia / Trans-Olza as a region), 'Orava' and 'Spisz' (regions); the Cieszyn and Trans-Olza regions use a coordinate-and-radius fallback intersected with Moravskoslezsky. The 1919 shape is adjusted (Eastern Galicia and western Volhynia added); the 1920 shape holds the Riga frontier for the Kyiv and Warsaw episodes. Lithuanian and Polish claims overlap at Vilnius in both Cliopatria shapes (13 of 23 cells within 40 km of Vilnius are in the Polish 1920 shape; 6 of 14 within 30 km in the Lithuanian). Six pages are cited (five budget plus the Vilnius Region page opened for the Lithuanian dossier).
